attacks.claim: TRAILING_PUNCT (/[.,;:!?)\]]+$/) is applied unanchored at the start to every URL match. On a long run of punctuation that is not at the end of the match, it backtracks quadratically. Descriptions are written by any neighbor and tokenized on every viewer's render, with no length cap. One crafted description (e.g. `http://a` followed by tens of thousands of `!` and then a letter) can freeze the item page for everyone who opens it.
attacks.evidence: const TRAILING_PUNCT = /[.,;:!?)\]]+$/; ... const raw = m[0].replace(TRAILING_PUNCT, ''); ABSENT: any input length cap before tokenize(text)

attacks.claim: A leading link is kept whole when collapsing, so a very long first URL leaves the collapsed view tall. This works against the PR's goal of bringing the 'Request to borrow' button up on phones. Nothing in the diff adds overflow-wrap or word-break, so long URLs or long unbroken words may also overflow the container under `white-space: pre-line`.
attacks.evidence: out.push(t); // a leading link is shown whole rather than collapsing to nothing; ABSENT: overflow-wrap/word-break CSS

attacks.claim: The limit is measured in UTF-16 units in the main path but in code points in the fallback branch. The PR text also claims truncation only cuts at whitespace or between tokens, but the fallback hard-cuts mid-word.
ItemDescription keeps `expanded` in useState without being keyed by item. If the component instance is reused for a different item, the new description inherits the old expanded state.

Stripping every trailing ')' truncates balanced URLs such as Wikipedia-style `Foo_(bar)`, so they link to the wrong address. URL_RE also does not exclude commas, so two URLs separated only by a comma merge into one link.
